full_judgment: 6. Mr. Nurul Huq submitted that this case arises out of a land dispute and there are numerous proceedings between the parties such as Misc, Case No. 49 of 1975 under section 143 (a) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and in view of this the matter does not come under Special Powers Act nor the police submitted its report under that Act and therefore, cognizance by the Special Tribunal was illegal. There is a considerable force in this argument. Section 27 of the Special Powers Act provides the procedure of the Special Tribunal and further provides that it shall not take cognizance of any, such offence except on a report in writing made by a Police Officer not below the sank of S.T. Section 190 of the Cr.P.C. provides three modes of taking cognizance namely, (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitutes such offence, (b) upon a report in writing of such facts made by any Police Officer, (c) upon information received from any person other than a Police Officer or upon his own knowledge or suspicion that such offence has been committed. Putting section 190 Cr.P.C. in juxtaposition to section 27 of the Special Powers Act, the conclusion is the law has provided for taking cognizance only upon a report in writing made by a Police Officer and not otherwise and therefore any cognizance taken on (a) or (c) of section 190 Cr.P.C. is not contemplated to the case of Khorshed Alam vs. State 27 D.L.R. 111, a Division Bench of this Court considered the question of taken cognizance under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 which provided for taking cognizance under two circumstances namely:
